A first stop before [Classic Synths Compared](synth-compare.qmd). Short sections, one idea each. Click a heading to fold or open it.

::: {.ik-do}
**What you'll do**

1. Read what the OB-Xa is and when it was made.
2. Learn its sound, one idea at a time.
3. Take a guided tour: press each **▶ Hear step** button and listen for one change.
4. Find records it is on.
5. Check yourself with a short quiz.
:::

## What it is

- The **OB-Xa** was made by **Oberheim** and "released in December 1980" (Wikipedia, "Oberheim OB-Xa").
- It has up to **eight voices**, and can split the keyboard or double the voices (OB-Xa manual, p. 13).
- It used Curtis chips for its oscillators and filters, which made it cheaper to build and fix than Oberheim's earlier synths (Wikipedia).

## Its sound

- **Two oscillators** a voice, with **sync** (OB-Xa manual, p. 10).
- Its filter switches between **2-pole (12 dB)** and **4-pole (24 dB)** (manual, p. 11). 2-pole is brighter and softer.
- **Unison** stacks the voices on one note (manual, p. 8).
- Oberheim's older **SEM** module had a filter with low-pass, band-pass, high-pass and notch (Wikipedia, "Oberheim SEM"); the OB-Xa does not.

## The panel

This is the OB-Xa panel from [Classic Synths Compared](synth-compare.qmd), drawn after the real one (not a copy). Play it from the keys under the panel, the computer keys (a w s e d f t g y h u j k) or a MIDI keyboard. Turn any knob while you play. The sound is this site's own model; nobody has compared it with the real instrument.

## Guided tour

Each step loads a worked example and changes one thing.

```{=html}
<div class="ik-step" data-ex="ob-2pole" data-set="{&quot;pole4&quot;:true}"><p><b>4-pole brass pad.</b> The filter on 4-pole (24 dB). Listen: smooth and dark.</p></div>
<div class="ik-step" data-ex="ob-2pole"><p><b>2-pole.</b> Flip to 2-pole (12 dB). Listen: brighter and more open: the famous Oberheim brass.</p></div>
<div class="ik-step" data-ex="ob-sync" data-set="{&quot;uni&quot;:false,&quot;sync&quot;:false,&quot;fEnvO2&quot;:false}"><p><b>Two oscillators, no sync.</b> Oscillator 2 a fifth above. Listen: a plain lead.</p></div>
<div class="ik-step" data-ex="ob-sync" data-set="{&quot;uni&quot;:false}"><p><b>Sync on.</b> Oscillator 2 synced, with the filter envelope moving its pitch (F-ENV → osc 2, manual p. 10). Listen for the tearing sweep.</p></div>
<div class="ik-step" data-ex="ob-sync"><p><b>Unison.</b> Every voice on the same note. Listen: very big.</p></div>
<div class="ik-step" data-ex="ob-sem-bp"><p><b>Not an OB-Xa: the SEM band-pass.</b> This filter mode is from the older SEM, not the OB-Xa. Listen: thin and nasal, low and high both cut.</p></div>
```

## Famous records

Named in Wikipedia, "Oberheim OB-Xa":

- Van Halen, "Jump" (1984)
- also used by Miles Davis, Prince and Queen

## Check yourself

Click an answer. You will see at once if it is right. Nothing is saved or sent.

```{=html}
<div class="ik-q" data-a="2"><p><b>How many voices can an OB-Xa have?</b></p><ul><li>One</li><li>Four</li><li>Eight</li><li>Thirty-two</li></ul><p class="ik-why">Manual p. 13.</p></div>
<div class="ik-q" data-a="0"><p><b>Which filter setting is brighter?</b></p><ul><li>2-pole (12 dB)</li><li>4-pole (24 dB)</li><li>They sound the same</li><li>Neither</li></ul><p class="ik-why">Fewer poles take away less.</p></div>
<div class="ik-q" data-a="0"><p><b>Which famous song has the OB-Xa as its main part?</b></p><ul><li>Van Halen, "Jump"</li><li>"Happy Birthday"</li><li>Beethoven's Fifth</li><li>"Planet Rock"</li></ul><p class="ik-why">Wikipedia.</p></div>
<div class="ik-q" data-a="0"><p><b>Band-pass, high-pass and notch are modes of…</b></p><ul><li>The older SEM filter</li><li>The OB-Xa filter</li><li>The keyboard</li><li>The LFO</li></ul><p class="ik-why">Step 6.</p></div>
```
